prompt: What question does an EDR ask that an antivirus does not?

choices.text: Whether a file on disk matches a known signature of malware
choices.why: That is the antivirus's own question.

choices.text: Whether what the machine does fits its job
choices.why: Right: behaviour, judged against what the machine is for.

choices.text: Whether the machine's packages are all at their latest versions
choices.why: That is vulnerability management, lesson 16.

choices.text: Whether a user's password is strong enough
choices.why: No part of EDR judges passwords.

prompt: Put the parts of an EDR in the order they work after something happens on a machine.
hint: The name lists most of them.
items: the sensor records the event as telemetry
a rule matches the telemetry and raises an alert
the machine is acted on: evidence, stop, isolate

prompt: After an alert, which question can an EDR answer and an antivirus that blocked the file cannot?

choices.text: Whether the file was malicious
choices.why: The antivirus answered that when it blocked it.

choices.text: Which signature matched, and which version of the database had it
choices.why: An antivirus logs exactly that.

choices.text: How to remove the file without rebooting
choices.why: Removal is the easy part, and both can do it.

choices.text: What started it, and whether the same thing happened on other machines
choices.why: Right: kept telemetry with parents, from every machine, answers it.

prompt: Inside web, `sudo auditctl -l` answers `Operation not permitted` although auditd is installed. Why?

choices.text: The kernel keeps one audit trail for the whole computer and never hands a container a piece
choices.why: Right. A product that needs it runs on the host, below the containers.

choices.text: sudo is not allowed to run auditctl
choices.why: sudo ran it as root; the kernel refused root inside a container.

choices.text: auditd has to be started first
choices.why: Starting it fails the same way, which is why build disabled it.

choices.text: The rules file is empty
choices.why: An empty list would print "No rules", not an error.

prompt: A process calls itself `[kworker/0:1]` in its arguments. Which field of the sensor's record shows what it really is?

choices.text: cmd, because it holds the full command line the process was started with
choices.why: A process can rewrite its own arguments, so cmd says what it wants.

choices.text: user, since kernel threads run as root
choices.why: Any root process would pass that test.

choices.text: ppid, because a real kernel worker has parent 2
choices.why: A useful hint, and still not what the program is.

choices.text: exe
choices.why: Right: the kernel's link to the program file, which the process cannot change.

prompt: Match each field of the sensor's record to the question it answers.

pairs.right: which program file is being run

prompt: Twenty runs of /bin/true left no line in sensor.jsonl. What does that say about the sensor?
hint: How does it find new processes?

choices.text: It ignores programs under /usr/bin on purpose
choices.why: No line of it filters by path; sleep from /usr/bin was recorded.

choices.text: It had crashed by then, because /bin/true writes nothing it could read
choices.why: The sleep that followed was recorded, so it was running.

choices.text: Programs run by ana are not recorded
choices.why: Its first line was ana's sleep 1.

choices.text: It looks every 0.2 s and misses what ends in between
choices.why: Right: polling has a gap, and a fast process falls through it.

prompt: Why does the lesson put sensor.py in /usr/local/sbin, which needs sudo to write?

choices.text: Because systemd-run only starts programs from sbin
choices.why: systemd-run starts any path it is given.

choices.text: Because Python refuses to run scripts from a home directory
choices.why: detect.py runs from ana's home without trouble.

choices.text: So that only root changes what it records
choices.why: Right: a sensor anyone can edit records whatever they want.

choices.text: Because files in sbin are kept when the lab is reset
choices.why: Every up throws the whole copy away, sbin included.

prompt: Why does the sensor write one JSON object per line rather than one big JSON document?

choices.text: Each line is read, appended and shipped on its own
choices.why: Right: jq and log shippers read it a line at a time.

choices.text: Because JSON documents may not be longer than one line
choices.why: JSON can span any number of lines.

choices.text: Because Python's json module can only write single lines
choices.why: It writes indented documents with indent=.

choices.text: To keep the file small enough to fit in memory on a server
choices.why: The format does not change the size much; the reason is how it is read.

prompt: Which of these is written the way this lesson's rules are written?

choices.text: Alert when nginx's workers start any program
choices.why: Right: nginx never needs to, whatever the program is.

choices.text: Alert when a file's SHA-256 is on a list of known malware
choices.why: That is a signature, lesson 7's tool.

choices.text: Alert when a process uses more than half of the processor
choices.why: That is a performance alarm, and it fires on every busy hour.

choices.text: Alert on every process started as root
choices.why: Root starts processes all day; nobody would read those alerts.

prompt: The alert for /tmp/update has nothing after `under`. What happened?
hint: When did the sensor look, and who was the parent then?

choices.text: The program hid its parent from /proc
choices.why: It is a copy of sleep; it hides nothing.

choices.text: detect.py drops parents for programs in /tmp, to keep the line short
choices.why: The rule prints the parents of every match.

choices.text: Its shell ended first, so process 1 had adopted it before the sensor looked
choices.why: Right: the chain stops at pid 1, so the list is empty.

choices.text: sudo removes the parent chain of the processes it starts
choices.why: The first two alerts show sudo in their chains.

prompt: The hunt lists processes 190, 191 and 193 for the portal's account. What was 192 most likely?
hint: Read the command the shell ran.

choices.text: A process another user started
choices.why: Nothing else was running commands on web at that second.

choices.text: A kernel thread, which has no program file
choices.why: Kernel threads are not numbered inside the container's process space.

choices.text: The sensor itself restarting after the download
choices.why: It ran without a break: the lines on both sides of the gap are its own.

choices.text: The cp, too quick for the sensor
choices.why: Right: it ran between curl and /tmp/update and ended between two looks.

prompt: Put the response to the /tmp/update alert in the order the lesson does it.
hint: The instinct is to do the second one first.
items: restore the machine to a known-good state
trap: Killing first destroys the one thing that could say what the process was.

prompt: Why hash /proc/<pid>/exe rather than /tmp/update?

choices.text: Because /tmp is not readable by root
choices.why: Root reads /tmp like anything else.

choices.text: It is the program actually running, even if the file is deleted or replaced
choices.why: Right: the path can change under you; the running image cannot.

choices.text: Because sha256sum cannot read files in /tmp
choices.why: It reads any file it has permission for.

choices.text: Because the two give different hashes
choices.why: While nothing has changed, they give the same one.

prompt: Why isolate a machine rather than switch it off?

choices.text: Memory, processes and logs survive for the responders
choices.why: Right: a power cut destroys exactly what the examination needs.

choices.text: Switching it off would break the portal for the firm's clients
choices.why: Isolation breaks the portal for them as well.

choices.text: A container cannot be switched off
choices.why: hostlab.sh down switches them all off.

choices.text: Isolation also removes whatever was on the machine
choices.why: It removes nothing; it only cuts the network.

prompt: isolate.nft drops everything in and out except loopback and one service with one machine. Which TCP port is that service on?
hint: The responder logs in from admin.

prompt: While isolate.nft was loaded, your shell on web kept working. Why?
hint: How does hostlab.sh reach a machine?

choices.text: Because the table exempts the connections that were already open
choices.why: Nothing in it mentions connection state.

choices.text: Because nftables leaves root's own traffic on the machine unfiltered
choices.why: It filters root's packets like anyone's.

choices.text: The shell enters the machine directly, with no network involved at all
choices.why: Right: much like an agent's own channel to its console.

choices.text: Because the lab computer's address is allowed by the second rule
choices.why: Only admin's address is allowed, and only for SSH.

prompt: How does a product's sensor avoid the gap that let /bin/true through?

choices.text: The kernel calls it, through eBPF or callbacks, when a program starts
choices.why: Right: nothing is too short, and the parents are still alive.

choices.text: By polling /proc a thousand times a second instead of five
choices.why: Faster polling narrows the gap and never closes it.

choices.text: By scanning every file on the disk once an hour
choices.why: That finds files, not processes that have already ended.

choices.text: By keeping a copy of every program that is installed
choices.why: A copy says nothing about what ran.

prompt: Match each weakness of the lesson's EDR to what a product does about it.

pairs.right: tamper protection, and silence as an alert

pairs.left: telemetry kept on the machine itself
pairs.right: records sent off the machine as they are made
a button in the console, or an automatic action

prompt: A firm buys an EDR and switches every rule on. Two months later nobody reads the alerts. What was skipped?

choices.text: Buying more licences, so every machine reports
choices.why: More machines would mean more unread alerts.

choices.text: Turning on automatic isolation for every rule
choices.why: Isolating on rules that fire on normal work would stop the business.

choices.text: Tuning
choices.why: Right: deciding, alert by alert, what is this firm's normal.

choices.text: Uninstalling the antivirus, which competes with the EDR for events
choices.why: The two run together on most machines; that is not why alerts go unread.

prompt: A company runs forty containers on one host and wants process telemetry from all of them. Where should the sensor run?

choices.text: Inside each container, one sensor per container
choices.why: Each would see what this lesson's sensor saw, without the kernel's events.

choices.text: On a separate machine that scans the containers over the network
choices.why: A scan sees ports, never processes.

choices.text: On the host, below the containers, where the kernel is
choices.why: Right: one sensor there sees every container's processes as they start.

choices.text: In the image, so every new container starts with one
choices.why: Still one sensor per container, with the same blind spots.

prompt: Which of these would make good rules for web's portal account? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does the portal's job never need?

choices.text: portal starts ssh or scp
choices.why: The portal never connects to other machines.

choices.text: portal runs python3
choices.why: That is the portal itself, all day.

choices.text: portal starts a program from /dev/shm
choices.why: Nothing legitimate runs from there.

choices.text: nginx's workers read files in /var/www
choices.why: Serving files is nginx's job.

prompt: Cutting a machine off the network except for the responders, while keeping it running, is called ___.
The sensor sleeps 0.2 s between looks. How many times a second does it look?
